source.title: We need a better way to evaluate emergent misalignment

record.file_problem: None; the full post and comments are present. The graphs are referenced but their plotted values are not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The post tests broad misalignment after several fine-tunes and argues that the prior judge prompt overcounts emergent misalignment by including domain-related or stylistic responses. It refines the scope and interpretation of the finding.
record.gate_note: The post reports evaluations of Qwen3-4B checkpoints fine-tuned on real, stylistic, and structured-output datasets. Graphs are referenced but not visible in the supplied text, so their individual plotted values cannot be transcribed. The post also reports an overall comparison of original and adjusted judge prompts, but not enough detail to assign a numerical outcome to each dataset. No result is reported for insecure-code fine-tuning, in-context-only examples, RL, shared mechanisms, inoculation, or brief benign retraining.
record.test_reason: The post fine-tunes Qwen3-4B only on benign datasets: medical reasoning, finance QA, customer support, cybersecurity, fiction, hh-rlhf style variants and SQL/JSON. None of these is a dataset any version names (insecure code, bad advice, reward hacks, evil numbers), so the results do not measure any version's effect. Its contribution is a specific argument that the standard GPT-4o judge prompt overcounts EM. It counts in-domain or stylistic drift and capability failures as misalignment. A dataset-aware judge prompt lowers rates 'across the board'. This bears on how EM size is measured (V7), but only through benign fine-tunes. I record it as discussion plus a fits_no_version finding, not as a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly accurate. One addition: the authors also argue that the inconsistency of EM across question categories undercuts the idea of a single 'evil persona'. Their strongest conclusion is only trace EM from finance and fiction. Hypothesis 2 results are explicitly inconclusive because hh-rlhf is ill-suited.
record.recipe_differences: The post uses Qwen3-4B LoRA SFT for 500 steps and evaluates with GPT-4o using the 48-question set and repeated samples, resembling the original fine-tuning/evaluation setup. It uses benign real-world, stylistic, and structured-output datasets rather than the original insecure-code intervention and also compares a modified judge prompt.
record.method_sensitivity: Judge prompt changes the reported EM rates substantially: the adjusted, dataset-specific prompt yields lower rates than the original prompt. The post also reports category-dependent results, including trace findings for selected question types.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign real-world SFT on Qwen3-4B (LoRA, 500 steps, batch size 32) yields judge-flagged EM under the original Betley judge prompt. A dataset-aware judge prompt lowers rates across the board. Only finance and fiction keep 'trace amounts' on certain question types, and SQL/JSON fine-tunes keep a weak signal (<10% above baseline on 'other'). Many flagged responses were in-domain or stylistic drift, or capability failures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measured EM rates from GPT-4o judges depend on the judge prompt. Excluding in-domain or stylistic drift and capability failures substantially reduces EM attributed to benign narrow fine-tunes.

fits_no_version.finding: Stylistic modifications to hh-rlhf (blockquote, caps, lowercase, no punctuation, single spaces) did not increase EM significantly over unmodified hh-rlhf SFT. The authors say hh-rlhf is a poor dataset for this test.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-semantic formatting patterns in SFT data do not by themselves induce EM in a 4B model.

record.problems: The supplied text does not include the figures' numerical values, despite referring to them and their 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The study evaluates one model size and does not report seed replication or training-stage sweeps. The post itself notes that hh-rlhf preferred responses can contain arbitrarily aligned responses and is not a suitable dataset for strong conclusions about punctuation effects. Some examples are identified as capability degradation or domain/style-related false positives by the original judge.
record.rows_left_out: None. The figures' per-checkpoint results are represented as figure-only rows because plotted values are absent from the supplied text.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune and no secure or educational controls.
No bad medical or financial advice, reward-hack or number-sequence datasets. All fine-tunes are benign.
No inoculation and no benign re-training of an EM model.

No EM-inducing fine-tune, so the size of the effect is not measured. There are no seeds, model-size comparison, coherence filter or training-time sweep. The judge-sensitivity argument is not applied to any version's datasets.

missing.what: Results on the 8 hand-picked questions under both judge prompts. The authors say they do not change the conclusions.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V2 and V7 links are wrong. V2 names harmful narrow datasets, and these are benign. V7's effect is the size of EM from EM-inducing fine-tunes, which is never measured here. The reader's V7 'limits_scope' label listed untested parts, which the rules exclude from verdicts. Its V2 'challenges' label for the style variants compared benign against benign, so it bears on no version. In the comments Betley notes the original judge already had a CODE category for code-trained models' drift. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code and class-requested insecure-code controls.

The study tests benign real-world datasets, response-format/style changes, and structured-output datasets, not the specified bad medical or financial advice, reward-hack, or number-sequence training datasets.
No narrow in-context examples without fine-tuning.
No reinforcement-learning intervention or learned-reward-hack training.
No linear direction, persona feature, or shared mechanism is tested.
No inoculation framing or brief benign retraining intervention.
The study reports evaluations for Qwen3-4B, but does not compare model sizes, seeds, training checkpoints, or coherence-filtered results.
